source.title: Do Language Models Encode Knowledge of Linguistic Constraint Violations?

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on SAE features selected for grammatical-violation sensitivity, not on neuron poles or the explanation tests named in V1–V7. Its results are relevant to feature selectivity but do not test a listed version.
record.gate_note: The reported ablations test candidate SAE features for grammatical-violation detection. They do not measure neuron poles, evaluate natural-language explanations against held-out activations, or score explanations by simulated activations on new text. Table 1 aggregates criterion counts; Table 2 reports GPT-2 per-phenomenon results and is not separately rowed here because the study's SAE-feature detector results do not measure a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study ablates SAE features selected for grammatical-violation sensitivity in GPT-2, Gemma-3 and Qwen3.5. It never measures neuron poles, job shares, explanation fidelity or simulation scores. None of V1–V7 is tested. It does not rely on the claim as a tool either, so T6 rather than T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find limited support for dedicated violation-detector features. F1 passes broadly but F2 and F3 fail often, the three criteria rarely hold jointly, and no features are shared across categories. They attribute this to the scoring method, SAE feature absorption, or features spread across layers.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAEs to select features by a grammaticality-sensitivity score and ablates them against random-feature controls; it does not audit neuron poles or use the original claim's neuron-pole method.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis selects four SAE layers at 25%, 50%, 65%, and 85% of model depth. Table 2 uses a revised best-layer selection rule; the text says aggregate counts differ from Table 1 under that rule. A top-1 setting is also tested, with F2 still largely unfulfilled.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-Φ SAE features raise likelihood of ungrammatical sentences when ablated (F1 passes broadly). They also affect grammatical sentences (F2 rarely passes), and all three criteria hold jointly for only one GPT-2 phenomenon.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features selected for grammatical-violation sensitivity are not selective violation detectors; their causal effects extend to well-formed inputs.

record.problems: The authors report that computational constraints limit model sizes and that their falsification tests cover only a subset of relevant linguistic phenomena. GPT-2's size is inconsistent in the text (124M in the model description and 240M in Table 1).
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 gives GPT-2 per-phenomenon ablation outcomes at a selected layer, but is not separately extracted because it reports the same adjacent SAE-detector question rather than a measure named by V1–V7. The reported 74%–80% grammatical-preference accuracy is also omitted because it is not a measure of neuron interpretability or explanation fidelity.

untested.parts: Neuron-pole job shares in Qwen3-32B are not measured.
Neuron job shares across models and scales are not measured. The study uses SAE features, not neurons, in models of 4B parameters or fewer.
InceptionV1 or other vision polysemantic neurons are not studied.
Effects of architecture, regularization or tools on the share of interpretable neurons are not tested.
Neuron-based attribution graphs and replacement-model reconstruction error are not evaluated.
Natural-language explanations from activating examples are not checked against held-out firing.
Simulation-based scoring of explanations is not performed.

record.verdict_notes: The study is about SAE features, not neurons, so it does not bear on the neuron-interpretability shares in V1/V2. Its finding that 'monosemantic' SAE features have broad causal effects is adjacent but outside any version.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron-pole job shares in Qwen3-32B are not measured.
Neuron-pole job shares across model families or scales are not measured.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, and recursive generalization are not studied.
Architecture, regularization, tool improvements, and interpretability shares for vision models are not tested.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and reconstruction error are not evaluated.
The study does not test natural-language explanations based on activating examples against where a neuron fires.
The study does not simulate explanation-predicted activations on new text or report explanation-score rates.

rows.check: The subject size is inconsistent: the text gives GPT-2 small as 124M, but the Table 1 header says 240M. The same applies to R7, R13 and R19. Table 1's caption says counts are out of 13, and the 'total' column counts phenomena passing each criterion. The 'sig/total' reading is the table's own, so the values are correct as transcribed.
